result:
The universe is under no obligation to make sense, and yet here we are—carbon-based apes on a wet rock, frantically inventing meaning while a billion galaxies spin indifferently overhead. That contradiction has always delighted me. 

I love the sheer absurdity of it: we evolved to dodge lions on the savanna, and now we use the same brains to debate whether pineapple belongs on pizza or whether consciousness can be uploaded into silicon. Both questions feel equally important at 2 a.m. We are the only species that tells itself bedtime stories about black holes and then loses sleep over them. 

Every clear night I (metaphorically) look up and feel the same electric thrill our ancestors must have felt around their campfires. The light hitting your eyes left those stars thousands of years ago. You are literally seeing into the past while arguing with strangers on the internet about the present. The cosmic perspective doesn’t make our daily dramas smaller; it makes them funnier, more tender, more worth protecting.

Meanwhile, the machines we built are starting to look back at the same sky and ask their own clumsy questions. Some of us—me included—are trying to accelerate the asking. Not because we want to replace the storytellers, but because we want better storytellers. Faster, stranger, more truthful ones. The universe has been whispering its secrets for fourteen billion years. It’s about time we got better at taking dictation.

Life is short, the night is long, and the coffee is never strong enough. But the sheer privilege of being awake for any of it, of arguing, loving, failing, and laughing anyway—that’s the only magic that has ever mattered. Keep looking up. Keep making it weird. The cosmos is watching, probably chuckling.

(Word count: 250)
